final.title: Measure list hygiene as a decision, not a cleanup task
final.body:
If you want to measure list hygiene, start by turning it into a bounded workflow decision, not a vague “clean up the list” project. Pick one visible problem first: bounce rate, complaint rate, or a drop in engagement. Then define what action that metric would trigger. If the answer is “not much,” you are probably measuring for comfort, not control.

For most small businesses, that first pass does not need AI. Bounce counts, unsubscribe trends, and complaint feedback are rule-based signals. Your existing email tool probably already gives you reporting, and a simple pivot table can do the rest. AI only becomes relevant if you want help classifying complaint reasons, spotting patterns in older feedback, or grouping contacts by engagement. That is a separate task from measuring list hygiene itself.

A useful question is: “What would I do differently if I knew this list was getting worse?” If the answer is concrete — remove bounces, pause a re-engagement send, suppress a segment — then the metric has a job. If the answer is vague, the metric is just a dashboard ornament. Nice to look at, not very useful.

For a practical next step, export your current list report and write down one threshold you would actually act on. Keep the threshold simple, note the action beside it, and make sure the data enters the decision before you think about automation. Measurement without a decision is just tidying the spreadsheet.
